world_behind.title: Some of them believed
world_behind.text: Verse 1 is easy to read past. Many believed, repented, and began to search the scriptures. The chapter that follows is about the rest, and the record makes sure the reader knows the preaching worked before it reports what it cost.

world_behind.title: The charge is reviling the law
world_behind.text: Verse 5 has the people witnessing that Alma and Amulek reviled the law and the lawyers and judges. Amulek had said in so many words that he spoke in favor of their law. The trial proceeds on the accusation the accused already answered.

world_behind.title: Zeezrom breaks first, and publicly
world_behind.text: He does not slip away. He cries out that he is guilty and that these men are spotless, pleads for them, and is spat on and cast out for it. His conversion costs him the city inside a single verse.

world_behind.title: The records burn with the people
world_behind.text: Verse 8 puts the holy scriptures into the same fire as the wives and children. A city destroying its own text alongside those who believe it is a detail the record chose to keep, and it makes the burning an act against memory as much as against persons.

world_behind.title: The judge belongs to Nehor
world_behind.text: Verse 16 identifies him with the order and faith of Nehor, who killed Gideon in Alma 1. The record ties this scene back to the first chapter of the book, so the reader knows the priestcraft introduced there is now sitting on a bench.

world_behind.title: Prison here is deprivation
world_behind.text: They are struck, questioned, mocked for days, denied food and water, and stripped. The record lists the treatment plainly and without adjectives, and the list runs several days long.

world_behind.title: The date is given to the day
world_behind.text: Verse 23 supplies the twelfth day of the tenth month of the tenth year. The record dates the deliverance the way it dated Amulek's conversion four chapters ago, fixing the moment to the day.

words.text: Secretly, out of sight. In the King James Bible it is the word for laying an ambush: lurking, waiting for blood, bringing in false teachers unnoticed. It has one famous gentle use, when Joseph is minded to put Mary away privily to spare her. Ammonihah "sought to put them away privily" (v. 3) in the same construction and the opposite spirit.

cites.quote: sought to put them away privily

spans.text: sought to put them away privily

words.text: Without blemish, the old requirement for anything offered. Zeezrom says "I am guilty, and these men are spotless before God" (v. 7), which is a sacrificial word applied to two men about to be bound. The sentence divides the room into one man who knows what he is and two who are about to be treated as offerings.

cites.quote: I am guilty, and these men are spotless before God

spans.text: I am guilty, and these men are spotless before God

words.text: Death for a testimony, and here the name of a place: they were carried "to the place of martyrdom" (v. 9). The word is absent from the King James Bible and appears twice in this record. Its use as an address implies a city with a customary spot for this.

Grinding the teeth, the gesture of rage in the older books and of torment in the gospels. Here the tormentors do it while asking "How shall we look when we are damned?" (v. 21), which puts the gesture of the damned on the faces of the people mocking. The record does not comment on the irony.

cites.quote: How shall we look when we are damned?

spans.text: How shall we look when we are damned?

words.text: Two. The walls of the prison "were rent in twain" (v. 27), and rent in twain is the exact phrase Matthew uses of the temple veil at the crucifixion. Both are barriers torn from top to bottom at a moment of death, and in both the tearing is what people see first.

phrases.term: Began to repent, and to search the scriptures
phrases.text: The first thing the chapter reports is success. Belief, repentance, and then reading, in that order. The verse also explains where the church at Sidom later in this book comes from.

phrases.term: I am guilty, and these men are spotless before God
phrases.text: Zeezrom's whole conversion in one sentence, and it takes the form of public testimony. He confesses in public, on the record, to the people he misled. What it earns him is spitting and expulsion.

phrases.term: The Spirit constraineth me that I must not stretch forth mine hand
phrases.text: The hardest sentence in the chapter, and it is a restraint, not an inability. Alma has the power and is being held back from using it. The verse gives the reason without softening it: the Lord receives them in glory, and the deed is being allowed so that the judgments may be just.

phrases.term: Our work is not finished; therefore they burn us not
phrases.text: Alma's answer to whether they will die too, and it puts survival on usefulness. The same logic would have burned them the moment the work ended. Amulek gets no promise of safety, only of timing.

phrases.term: This judge was after the order and faith of Nehor
phrases.text: A single verse of identification that reaches back thirteen chapters. Nehor was executed in Alma 1 and his teaching outlived him well enough to seat a judge. The record is tracking an idea.

phrases.term: How shall we look when we are damned?
phrases.text: Said in mockery, and it is the chapter's grimmest line. They are quoting the doctrine back as a taunt while doing the thing it warns about. Nobody in the scene hears it as a question.

phrases.term: How long shall we suffer these great afflictions, O Lord?
phrases.text: The prayer that ends the imprisonment, and it opens with a complaint. Alma asks how long before he asks for strength, and the record keeps the complaint in. The petition that follows is for strength unto deliverance.

phrases.term: According to their faith which was in Christ
phrases.text: The explanation given twice in three verses. The power that broke the cords is credited to faith, and the object of the faith is named both times. The record is careful not to let the miracle stand on its own.

verses.label: v. 1–5
verses.title: Believers, and a charge
verses.text: Many believe and begin to search the scriptures. The rest want the preachers dead, first quietly and then by law. They are bound and taken to the chief judge, and the people testify that they reviled the law.

verses.label: v. 6–7
verses.title: Zeezrom turns
verses.text: He is astonished, then aware of the blindness he caused, then harrowed by his own guilt. He cries out that he is guilty and the prisoners are spotless. They ask whether he is possessed, spit on him, and throw him out.

verses.label: v. 8–10
verses.title: The fire
verses.text: Believing wives and children are cast in, and the scriptures with them. Alma and Amulek are brought to watch. Amulek asks how they can witness it and proposes using the power they have.

verses.label: v. 11–13
verses.title: The restraint
verses.text: Alma answers that the Spirit forbids it, that the Lord receives them in glory, and that the deed is permitted so that the judgments against the city will stand. Amulek asks whether they will burn too. Alma says the work is not finished.

verses.label: v. 14–17
verses.title: The judge
verses.text: He strikes them, says their God did not save the burned, and asks what they say for themselves. The record identifies his allegiance. They answer nothing, and he sends them to prison.

verses.label: v. 18–22
verses.title: Days of it
verses.text: Lawyers, judges, priests and teachers of Nehor's profession come to question them and get silence. The judge demands speech and gets silence. Then striking, gnashing, spitting, mockery, hunger, thirst and stripping, for many days.

verses.label: v. 23–29
verses.title: The prison falls
verses.text: On a dated day the leaders come and each in turn tells them to deliver themselves. When the last has spoken, they stand. Alma prays, the cords break, the earth shakes, the walls tear, and everyone who mocked them is killed by the fall. The two walk out unhurt.

chapter.title: The miracle is withheld first and given later
chapter.text: The same power that breaks the prison could have stopped the fire. The chapter puts the restraint before the rescue so that the reader cannot read the deliverance as evidence that God intervenes whenever he can.

chapter.title: The reason given is judgment
chapter.text: Alma says the deed is suffered so that the judgments upon the city may be just. It is a hard answer and the record supplies no softer one, then spends the next chapter and a half carrying it out.

chapter.title: Silence is the response to interrogation
chapter.text: Alma and Amulek answer nothing, repeatedly, over days. Amulek argued in chapter 10 and Alma preached in 12 and 13. Here the record shows two men who have said everything they were sent to say.

chapter.title: Zeezrom's conversion is complete before the chapter is half over
chapter.text: He accuses himself, defends the innocent, and is expelled. The book's most thorough turn belongs to the man who tried hardest to buy a denial.

chapter.title: The record keeps the complaint
chapter.text: Alma's prayer begins by asking how long. The book could have kept only the request for strength. It preserves the exhaustion in front of it.

chapter.title: Nehor is the through-line
chapter.text: Alma 1 introduced the teaching, Alma 14 finds it on the judgment seat and in the prison. The record is showing what an idea does over thirteen chapters.

chapter.title: Everything burned is replaceable except the people
chapter.text: The scriptures went into the same fire. The city that destroyed the text is destroyed in the next chapter but one, and nothing in the record suggests the two facts are unrelated.

applications.title: Accept that you may be held back
applications.text: Alma had the power and was stopped. When you are able to fix something and something in you says not to, that is a recognized position in this book and not a failure of faith.

applications.title: Confess to the people you misled
applications.text: Zeezrom did it out loud, to the crowd he had deceived, and it cost him. A private acknowledgment would have been easier and would not have been the same act.

applications.title: Say nothing when you have said everything
applications.text: Silence under questioning is a real answer here, chosen by men who had already spoken. Notice the difference between not having a reply and having finished giving one.

applications.title: Let the complaint into the prayer
applications.text: The record keeps "how long" in front of the petition. Try praying the honest first sentence before the acceptable second one, and see whether the second changes.

questions.text: When did a hard word actually work on me, and did I ever tell the person who said it?
What would I have to say in public, to people who heard me say the opposite, for a change in me to be real?
When have I been restrained from fixing something, and did I treat that as guidance or as failure?
If my safety lasts as long as my work does, what work am I actually doing?
What true thing have I repeated as a joke because taking it seriously would cost me something?
What is my honest first sentence to God right now, before the respectable one?
What have I credited to luck or timing that I would describe differently if I were being exact?
